results.title: Adjusted Rand Index - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) is defined as a measure used in cluster validation that computes the similarity between detected communities and "ground-truth" communities, ranging from -1 to +1. The Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) is a statistical measure designed to quantify the similarity between two clusterings, correcting for chance agreement between partitions. The adjustment for chance is what differentiates ARI from the Rand Index; ARI normalizes the index so that its expected value is zero when clusters are selected randomly and one when there is perfect agreement between partitions. The Adjusted Rand Index is known to be sensitive to the number of clusters in the partitions being compared, which can result in selection bias and higher values for clustering solutions with many clusters. The Jaccard Index is similar to ARI but does not consider pairs of data points in different clusters, and is defined as the ratio of pairs assigned to the same cluster in both partitions to the total number of pairs assigned to the same cluster in either partition. The Rand index measures the agreement between true clustering and predicted clustering: ARI normalizes, so the expected value is 0 when the clusters are selected by chance and 1 when a perfect match is achieved. Moreover, in order to evaluate and compare the performance of each clustering algorithm, (1) we utilized several clustering algorithms (agglomerative, k-means, and k-medoids), (2) the performance of each of the clustering algorithms is evaluated against a conducted ground truth at Alstom Sweden AB, and (3) the adjusted mutual information (AMI), normalized mutual information (NMI), and the adjusted rand index (ARI) are selected as performance metrics. For assessment of the methods, we use four popular effectiveness measures: ( i ) Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI) , which is an adjustment of the Mutual Information (MI) score to account for chance, ( ii ) Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) , which determines the Rand index (RI) score adjusted for chance, ( iii ) Boundary Recall (BR), which measures boundary adherence , and ( iv ) Cluster Accuracy , which measures the degree of intersection between predicted and ground-truth segmentation.

results.title: Guide to Confusion Matrices & Classification Performance Metrics | Towards Data Science
results.content: Confusion matrices can be used to calculate performance metrics for classification models. Of the many performance metrics used, the most common are accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. Normally, I wouldn’t use accuracy as a performance metric, I’d rather use precision, recall, or the F1 score. As stated earlier, accuracy is generally not a great metric to use for overall model performance, but it can be used to compare model outcomes while tuning your training data and finding optimal hyperparameter values. Recall, which measures the true positive rate, is a good metric to use when we are focusing on limiting our false negatives. I personally like to use the F1 score as my general performance metric unless the specific problem warrants using either precision or recall. from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score. In this article we described confusion matrices, as well as calculated by hand and with code, four common performance metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score.
